query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an alloying modification that promotes in-situ formation of a protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer will improve high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a TiVNbTa-based alloy) without an intentionally engineered protective oxide scale.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition by adding (or increasing the proportion of) chromium (Cr) and tantalum (Ta) in a way that enhances the formation of a CrTaO4-based oxide layer during high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Exposure at extreme temperatures, for example 1100 °C in an oxidizing (air) atmosphere, for extended durations (up to 200 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent CrTaO4-based oxide scale that forms on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The added Cr and Ta preferentially oxidize to form a stable CrTaO4-based scale at high temperature. This scale acts as a barrier that slows oxygen diffusion into the underlying alloy, thereby reducing further oxidation and degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to show a significantly reduced weight gain (oxidation rate) compared to a similar alloy without the Cr and Ta adjustment, indicating improved oxygen resistance under the test conditions.
generation.baseline: An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy which, when exposed to 1100 °C in air, develops a non-protective oxide scale with an exponential weight gain due to uncontrolled oxygen ingress.
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism is expected to work effectively only if the concentration of Cr and Ta exceeds a threshold necessary for continuous CrTaO4 phase formation; if the alloy's composition or processing conditions do not favor the formation of a coherent oxide scale, the oxygen resistance might not improve as predicted.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports the beneficial role of CrTaO4-based scales in improving oxidation resistance, the precise critical concentrations and quantitative magnitude of improvement require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set is a conventional refractory high-entropy alloy and the other set is modified with increased Cr and Ta to promote CrTaO4 formation. Expose both sets to 1100 °C in an air atmosphere for 200 hours. Characterize the surface and cross-sectional microstructures using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), alongside measuring weight gain due to oxidation.
measurements: Phase identification of surface oxides via XRD
Cross-sectional imaging and thickness measurement of the oxide scale (via SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrTaO4 oxide layer does not form on the modified alloy or if its oxidation weight gain is not significantly lower than that of the untreated control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
